cues.text: Chapter five is about the tools for engagement and personalisation.
Let us begin with a simple question.
Once an organisation has decided that it wants to build better relationships with its customers, what actually helps it do that day to day?
The answer is a set of digital tools, and each one has a clear role and a clear risk.
Good digital leaders learn both together.
Let us walk through a table that lists seven tools.
The table has three columns.
The first column is Tool.
The second is Role, meaning what the tool does for the organisation.
The third is Examples and risks, meaning the products you may have heard of, and the dangers you must manage.
I will take the rows in order.
Row one is the CRM.
CRM stands for Customer Relationship Management.
Its role is to hold, in one central place, the customer interactions, the cases, and the preferences.
Think of a bank or a telecom company.
Without a CRM, one staff member may not know what another staff member promised the same customer last week.
With a CRM, the history is shared.
The examples given are Salesforce and HubSpot.
The risk is that you must protect customer records, because a CRM concentrates a great deal of personal information in one place.
Row two is email marketing.
Its role is segmented campaigns and automated communication.
Segmented means different groups receive different messages, rather than everyone receiving the same one.
Automated means certain messages are sent without a person pressing send each time, for example a welcome message after sign-up.
The example given is Mailchimp.
The risks are that you must avoid spam, and avoid excessive tracking of what recipients do.
Row three is social tools.
Their role is to coordinate outreach and to listen to feedback.
So they work in two directions: you send messages out, and you also pay attention to what people are saying back.
The examples are Hootsuite and Buffer.
The risk is response quality, so you must manage how well, how quickly and how appropriately the organisation replies.
Row four is live chat and chatbots.
Their role is real-time support, and automated answers to routine questions.
A routine question might be about opening hours or the status of an order.
The examples are Intercom and Zendesk.
The risk to manage is that you must provide human escalation.
That means a customer who is stuck or has a complicated problem must be able to reach a real person.
Row five is analytics.
Its role is to understand behaviour and to find bottlenecks in the customer journey.
A bottleneck is a point where customers slow down, get confused or give up.
The source gives web and app events as the examples, such as which pages are visited or which buttons are tapped.
The risks are consent and data quality.
Consent means people should agree to being tracked.
Data quality means that if the data is wrong or incomplete, your conclusions will be wrong too.
Row six is recommendation engines.
Their role is to suggest relevant offerings, such as a product, a video or a course that a customer is likely to want.
The risks listed are that you must avoid unfair targeting, and avoid filter bubbles.
A filter bubble happens when a person is shown only more of what they already like, so their view of the available choices becomes narrow.
Row seven is surveys and feedback tools.
Their role is to capture perceptions and suggested improvements, in other words what customers think and what they would like changed.
The risks are sample bias and fatigue.
Sample bias means the people who answer may not represent all your customers.
Fatigue means that if you ask too often, people stop answering or answer carelessly.
Now let us look at the methods that sit behind these tools.
The source names four ideas.
First, segmentation.
Segmentation groups customers by relevant characteristics.
The word relevant matters.
You group people by features that actually affect what they need, not by whatever happens to be easy to record.
Second, recommendations.
Recommendations may use content similarity, or collaborative patterns.
Content similarity means the system suggests items that resemble something you already used.
Collaborative patterns means the system looks at what other people with similar behaviour chose, and suggests that to you.
Third, predictive analytics.
This estimates needs or churn.
Churn means customers leaving or stopping their use of a service.
So predictive analytics tries to estimate what a customer will need next, or how likely they are to leave.
Fourth, A/B testing.
This compares variants with controlled assignment and predefined outcomes.
Suppose you have two versions of a message.
Controlled assignment means customers are allocated to version A or version B in a deliberate, controlled way.
Predefined outcomes means you decide in advance what you will measure, such as the proportion who respond, before you look at results.
The source then gives a warning: do not declare success from noisy or selectively chosen data.
Noisy data is data with so much random variation that a difference may be chance.
Selectively chosen data means picking only the results that look good.
Either one can make a failed idea look like a success.
Finally, the source brings these tools back to people.
A personalised service can combine relevant digital suggestions with human support for complex needs.
Digital suggestions handle the simple and the common cases well, while a human is better when a situation is complicated.
The source also lists what accessibility includes.
First, readable text.
Second, keyboard and screen-reader compatibility, so people who cannot use a mouse or cannot see the screen can still use the service.
Third, language support.
Fourth, bandwidth-friendly interfaces, meaning they work on slow or expensive connections.
Fifth, clear error recovery, meaning that when something goes wrong, the user is told plainly what happened and how to continue.
The source then gives a Nigerian context.
Nigerian rural services may benefit from offline support, from SMS and USSD where feasible, and from local language training.
SMS is text messaging.
USSD is the short-code menu system, where a person dials a code such as one beginning with a star and receives menu options on a basic phone, without needing a smartphone or a data connection.
Note the qualification: where feasible.
It will not always be possible.
The closing principle is this: do not remove human alternatives simply to increase digital usage.
A digital channel is a means of serving customers better, and it is not a goal in itself.
If a customer cannot or prefers not to use it, a human route must remain.
